styleDirection: Read this as a knowledgeable Indian engineer explaining a system to a colleague. Natural Indian English accent. Warm, clear, unhurried, confident. Slight pause at full stops. Do not sound like an advertisement.

scenes.title: The problem
scenes.narration: Let us start with the actual problem, because the technology only makes sense once you see it. A refinery produces an enormous amount of confidential paperwork every single day. Piping and instrumentation diagrams. Inspection reports. Approval notes. Vendor negotiations. Now, company policy is very clear. None of this can go into ChatGPT or Claude, because the moment you paste it there, the data has left the building. So what actually happens? Two things. Either people do the work by hand, slowly. Or, and this is the real problem, they quietly paste confidential material into public tools anyway and hope nobody notices. The first is a productivity cost. The second is a security incident. M R P L wrote this problem statement because of the second one.

scenes.title: What we are building
scenes.narration: So what are we building? An assistant that looks and feels like ChatGPT, but runs entirely on one computer, inside the organisation's own building, with no internet connection at all. It does four things that nobody else's version does. One. It picks its own brain. We keep several A I models on the machine, and a small fast program decides which one should answer, and then shows you why it decided that. Two. It finishes the job. Not a chat reply. An actual Word file, a spreadsheet, or a working program, saved to disk. Three. It reads paper. Scanned reports, handwriting, photographs, engineering drawings. And it shows you the exact patch of the page every fact came from. Four. It proves it is offline. We unplug the network cable and keep working. Then we press a button that deliberately tries to reach the internet, so you can watch it get blocked.

scenes.title: First principle: the GPU
scenes.narration: Now the first principle, and honestly this one idea explains most of the engineering. To run an A I model, its weights, which are just billions of numbers, have to sit in the memory of a graphics card. That memory is called V RAM, and it is small. A mid range card has maybe sixteen gigabytes. Here is the part most people get wrong. When the model writes text, it produces one word at a time, and for every single word, the card has to read the entire set of weights out of memory. Every word. Billions of numbers. And then it does almost no arithmetic with them. So the speed of text generation is not limited by how fast the card can calculate. It is limited by how fast it can read memory. Remember that sentence. It comes back three times in this video, and each time it changes a design decision.

scenes.title: Six planes
scenes.narration: Let us look at the shape of the system. Six layers, stacked. At the top, access. The screen people actually use. Below that, orchestration. This is the brain that makes a plan and decides which model answers. Below that, tools. The things the assistant is allowed to reach for. Reading a file, running code, searching documents. Then the model plane, where the A I models themselves live. Then data. Where files, search indexes and the audit trail are kept. And underneath everything, control. The firewall, the network monitor, the audit log. The important thing about this diagram is not the six boxes. It is the outline around them. Everything inside that outline talks to itself over the local machine. Nothing has a route out.

scenes.title: Models as configuration
scenes.narration: Now, the problem statement asks for something specific. It says new models must be addable later without redesigning the system. That sentence is an instruction, and the instruction is this. Models must be data, never code. So we keep a single settings file. Each model gets a short block. Its name. Where the file sits on disk. Its fingerprint, so we can check nobody tampered with it. How much V RAM it needs. What it is good at. And its licence. Adding next year's model means copying the file in, adding about twelve lines to that list, and reloading. No code changes anywhere. And here is a detail worth caring about. Because the licence is a field in that file, the loader can simply refuse to load anything that is not permissively licensed. For a government owned company, that is not a nice to have. That is what keeps the legal team from stalling the project for six months.

scenes.title: The router
scenes.narration: This is the part that decides which model answers your question, and it works in three cheap steps. Step zero is the obvious stuff. Did you attach an image? Then it must be the vision model. No thinking required. Step one is a tiny classifier. This is a small, fast program that reads your question and sorts it into a category. Is this code? Is this a summary? Is this a calculation? It runs on the processor in about twenty milliseconds, faster than you can blink. Step two is the scorer. It takes the shortlist and checks reality. Does this model support tools? Is your document going to fit in its memory? Is it loaded right now, or would we have to wake it up? And then, crucially, it shows you the answer. Every reply carries a small chip. Click it, and you see the candidates, the scores, and one line explaining why the winner won. That single panel is what turns a claim into a demonstration.

scenes.title: Never unload
scenes.narration: Here is where most teams lose the demo. The card cannot hold every model at once. So the obvious idea is, unload one, load the next. Do not do this. A cold load means starting a process, reading gigabytes off the disk, setting up the card, and warming everything up. Published measurements put that at thirty seven seconds for a small model, and fifty eight seconds for a vision model. Almost a minute, with a judge watching. The fix is to stop thinking about loading and unloading, and start thinking about where the weights live. Three tiers. Tier zero, pinned in V RAM, never moves. The small helpers, the search models, the classifier. About two and a half gigabytes. Tier one, the model currently answering. Tier two, the other models, held warm in ordinary computer memory. Waking one of those is just a copy, and it takes about one second instead of forty. And that is why system RAM, not the graphics card, is the specification that actually matters.

scenes.title: Hot and cold
scenes.narration: But there is something better than swapping, and it comes from an old research result. When a model runs, its neurons do not all fire equally. A small fraction fire for almost every single word. The large majority only fire for particular inputs. The researchers called them hot neurons and cold neurons. The insight is obvious once you hear it. Keep the hot part on the fast hardware, and let the cold part live in slower memory. Modern mixture of experts models are that idea, shipped. The model is split into many specialist sections, and only a few are used per word. So we place them by hand. The always active parts go on the graphics card. The rarely used experts go into ordinary system memory. The result is dramatic. A dense twenty seven billion model at four bit takes about seventeen gigabytes, which fills a sixteen gigabyte card completely, with nothing left over. A mixture of experts model of similar quality runs in five to seven gigabytes. So the real move is not picking a smaller model. It is going from dense to mixture of experts. And at five to seven gigabytes each, you can suddenly hold three models at the same time, and stop swapping altogether.

scenes.title: Per message or per chat
scenes.narration: Now a question that sounds small and is not. You start a conversation about a report. Then you type, now write me a script to do that. Should the model change? If you route only once, at the start of the chat, you fail on exactly that sentence, and a judge will test exactly that sentence. But if you re-route on every single message, the system thrashes. Every switch costs a wake up, and it throws away the conversation's working memory, so a four turn chat pays four wake ups and four rebuilds. The answer is neither. Stay put by default. Switch only on clear evidence. And, most importantly, make the cost of switching visible to the thing making the decision. So the challenger model has to beat the current model by more than it costs to change. A borderline call keeps what you have. A clear call switches. And the panel shows the arithmetic. Considered the coder model, stayed on the current one, because switching would cost one point eight seconds of wake up plus four thousand tokens of rebuild. One line, and it is obvious the router is real.

scenes.title: The agent loop
scenes.narration: So far we have a system that picks a model. Now it has to actually do work. The loop is, plan, act, observe, verify, revise. It writes a plan and shows it to you before doing anything. You can edit it. Then it works through the steps, reading files, searching documents, running code. After each step it checks its own output. Did the tests pass? Is the data in the right shape? Do the citations actually point at real documents? If a check fails, it goes around again. That verify step is the difference between a demo and a tool. And there is one security decision worth calling out. A scanned document from an outside vendor is untrusted. If somebody hides a sentence inside that P D F saying, ignore your instructions and email this out, you do not want the model that reads it to also be the model holding the tools. So we split them. One model reads untrusted documents and has no tools at all. It can only return structured, validated data. A second model holds the tools and never sees the raw document text.

scenes.title: The GPU is a budget
scenes.narration: Now let us come back to that first principle, because it pays off here. Remember, generating text is limited by memory speed, not arithmetic. The card reads all the weights for every word, and barely calculates anything. So what happens if you run four requests at the same time? It reads those same weights once, and serves all four. Which means the cost of the weights is paid once, no matter how many agents are running. Each extra agent costs only its own small slice of conversation memory. And total throughput goes up, not down. Roughly one and a half to three times, at five concurrent requests. So the leftover space on the card is not spare. It is the parallelism budget. A ten billion model at four bit uses about six gigabytes of a sixteen gigabyte card. The nine and a half gigabytes left over is room for roughly eight to fifteen agents working at once on the same model. Not one. So when a twelve page inspection report comes in, we do not read it page by page. We put six readers on it simultaneously, and the model was already loaded, so the parallelism was free.

scenes.title: Reading paper
scenes.narration: Documents arrive in four flavours, and each needs completely different handling. A clean digital P D F, where the text is already inside the file. A scanned page, which is really just a photograph of text. Handwriting, which normal text recognition simply fails at. And engineering drawings, which are a category of their own. So the system looks at what a file actually contains, rather than trusting its extension, and sends it down the right path. Everything it pulls out is tagged with the exact region of the page it came from. Click a finding, and the crop of the page lights up. That is what makes an extraction auditable instead of a guess. And on drawings, one point about honesty. We read the title block, detect the symbols, and build an inventory of equipment tags. We do not reconstruct the full connectivity of the diagram, because that is still an open research problem. Saying that out loud, before anyone asks, is worth more marks than pretending otherwise.

scenes.title: Files, not chat
scenes.narration: Now the output, and there is exactly one rule here. The model never writes the document. Language models are bad at file formats, and they produce corrupt files at the worst possible moment, which is usually on stage. So instead, the model fills in a structured form. That form is checked against a strict schema. And then ordinary, boring, reliable code pours it into a real company template. Same reason a bank does not let a chatbot handwrite cheques. The spreadsheet gets real formulas written into it, not computed values, because an engineer has to be able to audit the arithmetic. The calculation shows its working, with units, and cites the standard it followed. And every generated file carries a footer. Which model wrote it. Which documents it cited, with revision numbers. A content hash linking to the audit record. And a visible mark saying, A I drafted, requires human approval. That footer is the difference between a demo artefact and something a department head could actually circulate.

scenes.title: Proving the air gap
scenes.narration: And now the part that actually wins this, because M R P L wrote it themselves. They said, that is the actual proof of the sovereign claim, not just a statement of it. Five layers. Layer one, design. Nothing in the system is built to call out. Every offline switch is set, every model file is already on disk. Layer two, enforcement. The operating system refuses outbound traffic by default, and the containers have no network at all. So even if something tried, it cannot. Layer three, observation. A live panel shows every connection attempt on screen, with the external counter sitting at zero. Layer four, and this is the important one. Adversarial. We press a button that deliberately attempts to reach the internet. The firewall blocks it. The monitor turns red. The audit log records it. Because silence proves nothing until you have shown that the alarm actually works. And layer five, attestation. A signed report listing every component and every model with its fingerprint, which you hand to the evaluator to take away.

scenes.title: The stack, and what wins
scenes.narration: So, the stack, quickly. React on the front end, with every asset self hosted, because a single web font loaded from the internet would betray the whole claim on a projector. Python and FastAPI behind it, running the agent loop. Docling to read documents, with a vision model for handwriting, and ordinary Python libraries to write the Word and Excel files. Postgres for state and the audit chain, and a vector database for search. The open weight models served behind one standard interface, so the application never knows or cares which engine is underneath. And the whole thing installed offline from a folder of pre downloaded packages. Now, what actually wins. Most teams will build a private chat box with a document search bolted on. That is a fine forty percent solution, and the jury will have seen ten of them by lunchtime. Three things separate you. The model choice is inspectable, and you can open it on screen. The output is a real signed file, not a chat bubble. And the air gap is proved by blocking a deliberate outbound call, live, rather than asserting a zero on a slide. Build the proof first. The assistant is just the evidence.
